title: Wisdom with compassion
hookLine: if nobody's really there, why be kind? Shantideva writes the objection into his own poem, and answers it
tomorrow: a long poem ends. what do you do with the good it did?

lines: THE CRITIC IS IN THE POEM.
cards: Somebody in a group chat posts it at midnight: if there's no real self, then nobody's really getting hurt, right? It sounds clever at that hour. Here's the odd part.
Shantideva saw that exact move coming, and he wrote it into his own poem. In chapter nine an imagined critic asks him: if there are no beings, then who is compassion for?
He doesn't skip the question or change the subject. He answers it.

teach.b: His answer is short. Compassion is for beings as they appear in everyday life, the ordinary way of seeing that he keeps for the sake of the goal, which is ending suffering. That's the two truths again.
Ultimately, no fixed core. Conventionally, a friend crying in the hallway, and that's where kindness happens. But the chapter before goes further and turns the worry upside down.
If no one owns pain, Shantideva says, then nothing sorts it into mine and yours.

teach.h: PAIN WITH NO OWNER IS ALL ALIKE.
teach.b: Suffering without an owner is all alike, and it should be removed simply because it is suffering. So why guard only my own? Look at what that does.
The wall that made someone else's pain not my problem was the self. Take the wall down, and the pain doesn't disappear; it just stops being sorted. Seeing emptiness doesn't make the heart colder.
It makes it harder to look away. The tradition has two words for the pair.
Prajna, wisdom: seeing how things are. Karuna, compassion: the wish for suffering to end. Some Mahayana teachers call them the two wings of a bird, because one wing alone just flaps in a circle.
Wisdom without warmth turns into the clever midnight post. Warmth without wisdom burns out, or picks favorites. Shantideva wants both in the same breath.

how: In Mahayana Buddhism, wisdom and compassion are taught as a pair; students of the Bodhicaryavatara often study chapter eight's exchange of self and others alongside chapter nine's wisdom.

o: being smart enough to stay calm about others' problems
seeing clearly and caring more, the two together
the kindness that comes from knowing all the answers

p: nothing sorts it into mine and yours

s: seeing no self is supposed to make you cool and detached toward others
Shantideva argues the reverse: pain with no owner can't be sorted into mine and not mine.
Shantideva writes the objection 'who is compassion for?' into his own poem
an imagined critic asks it in chapter nine, and he answers: for beings as they appear in everyday life.
in this teaching, wisdom can work fine without compassion
the two go together, like two wings. wisdom alone turns clever and cold.

games.q: your little cousin hears about "no self" and grins: "so if I trip my brother, nobody's really hurt." what's Shantideva's answer?
o: the hurt is real in everyday life, and pain with no owner is everyone's to prevent.
he's right on the ultimate level, so it's only a rule about manners now.
no-self is too advanced for him; just say tripping is against the rules.
games.why: Shantideva keeps the everyday level: beings as they appear are who compassion is for. and with no owner, pain isn't someone else's problem.

practice: Let one person come to mind who's having a hard week. See their trouble plainly, without sorting it into theirs or yours, and without deciding whose fault it is. Then write them one kind sentence, even if it stays in your versions.

wordCard.voice: Wisdom with compassion: seeing there's no fixed self, and finding it harder, not easier, to look away from someone's pain.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: compassion, the wish that suffering end. In the Mahayana it's paired with prajna (प्रज्ञा), wisdom.

carryVoice: Keep this one: wisdom and warmth, two wings that only fly together. Day forty-five of the guide.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 9.75–9.76 (if no being exists, for whom is compassion? for beings as conventionally imagined, accepted for the sake of the goal)
Bodhicaryavatara 8.101–8.103 (sufferings without an owner are all alike; remove them because they are suffering)
